payload.name: PreserveExplicitQuotedClauses
payload.description: When constructing memory from a message containing a speaker's direct quoted statement, before accepting an extraction candidate, check that every explicit claim in the quoted text is represented, not only a paraphrase summary.
content: During extraction, when a source message is a direct quote (e.g., "John said ..."), compare the candidate memory content against the quoted utterance claim-by-claim.

If the candidate omits any explicit claim, especially a recommendation or assessment such as "you won't regret it," revise the candidate to include that claim, either in the same memory or as a separate memory entry.
Stop once all explicit claims are covered; do not add inferred implications or expand beyond the quoted text.

candidates.solves: The general failure is extraction candidates that paraphrase a speaker's quoted utterance and silently drop an explicit claim, causing later questions about that exact statement to be unsupported. This applies to future construction sessions where a message contains a direct quote with several distinct assertions, including evaluative or persuasive statements that a later question may target. It must not apply to ordinary conversational summaries that are not direct quotes or to exhaustively expanding paraphrase with inferred or general-knowledge content.

payload.name: Attribute relayed condition to the patient, not the speaker
payload.description: Use when extracting memories from a message where the speaker relays or acknowledges a fact about another participant's condition (e.g., a doctor's assessment said to the patient). Attribute the memory to that participant, not the speaker; keep separate subjects in separate candidates.
content: During extraction, when a message reports or acknowledges a condition fact about someone other than the speaker (e.g., 'the doctor said it's not too serious' in response to that person), create a separate state memory for that person, with the speaker only as source.
Resolve subject from pronouns and prior turns: 'your injury' refers to the addressee; a named person refers to that person. Do not merge facts about different subjects into one memory candidate.
If the same turn also contains the speaker's own state, emit distinct candidates per subject. Stop expanding further once each referenced person's fact has its own candidate.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often stores a fact about another participant's condition under the speaker, so the patient's state is missing. This skill applies when a message relays or acknowledges a doctor's or other assessment about the addressee or a named third party (e.g., John tells Tim 'the doctor said it's not too serious' after Tim's injury) and requires a separate memory attributed to that party. It does not apply when the message only describes the speaker's own condition or when the subject is already unambiguous.

payload.name: Extract first-person group behavior statements
payload.description: When a speaker uses first-person language to state a durable fact about their own or their group's behavior (e.g., 'we back each other up'), extract a candidate memory even if the statement appears inside a reply with thanks or filler.
content: During extraction, scan each message for explicit first-person statements about the speaker's own or their group's persistent behavior, traits, or approach (e.g., 'we back each other up', 'we won't quit').

When such a statement is found, create one durable candidate memory (typically a state or relationship) capturing the behavior, even if the statement is embedded in a reply that also contains thanks, pleasantries, or reactions to prior turns.
Do not create a candidate for transient, conversational, or purely reactive content (e.g., 'thanks', 'that's great') that does not state a durable fact.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that candidate extraction misses durable first-person statements about the speaker's or their group's behavior when they are embedded in conversational replies. This Skill applies when a future message contains an explicit first-person plural or singular statement of persistent behavior or approach (e.g., how a team handles tough opponents) that should become a memory. It does not apply to transient reactions, greetings, or purely conversational content that states no durable fact.

payload.name: Extract implied death from euphemistic loss language
payload.description: When a message describes someone with euphemistic permanent-loss phrases (e.g., 'will never be able to...', 'I miss him/her here'), use those cues during candidate extraction to record the implied state (likely deceased) as a hedged fact.
content: During candidate extraction, when a speaker refers to someone with euphemistic permanent-loss language—such as 'will never be able to support me' or 'I miss him/her here'—infer the implied state (likely deceased) and record it with hedged wording (e.g., 'likely no longer alive') instead of only the literal limitation.

Only apply this inference when the phrasing strongly implies permanent absence (e.g., 'never' combined with 'miss'); for temporary incapacity, mere distance, or estrangement, record only the literal limitation.
Do not state death as certain unless the message explicitly confirms it, and keep the memory evidence-bound by referencing the euphemistic phrase that supports the implication.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that extraction candidates omit strongly implied facts when the source uses euphemistic loss language, so later memory-based answers cannot address questions about that implied state. This Skill applies when a user describes someone with permanent-loss euphemisms (e.g., 'will never be able to support me' plus 'I miss him here') and a future question may ask whether that person is alive. It must not apply when the language only indicates temporary incapacity, distance, or estrangement, which do not imply death.

payload.name: Preserve_short_speaker_quotes_during_extraction
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates from a message that contains a short, distinctive verbatim quote from a speaker about an event or plan, preserve the exact quoted phrase in a memory candidate.
content: During extraction, if a message contains a short (roughly 2-15 words) verbatim quote from a speaker that is a standalone statement about an event or plan, create a memory candidate that includes the exact quoted phrase (as event or state memory), in addition to any abstract event/relationship summary.

Limit to one quote memory per speaker-message pair, only when the quote is distinctive enough that a future question could ask 'what did X say about Y'; skip generic, long, or conversational filler utterances.

candidates.solves: General failure mechanism: extraction summarizes a speaker's words into abstract event/relationship memories and drops the verbatim quote, so later questions asking for exact wording cannot be answered. Applies to future construction sessions where a message contains a short, distinctive, attributable quote about an event or plan. Does not apply to messages without direct quotes, long/ordinary statements, or questions requiring only gist.

payload.name: Extract Anaphoric Entity Descriptions
payload.description: When a message contains a declarative reply identifying an object, person, or place via a pronoun/demonstrative (e.g., 'It's a ...', 'That's my ...'), and the referent is clear from prior context, extract a memory candidate.
content: During extraction, create a candidate when a speaker's short reply identifies or describes an entity with a pronoun/demonstrative, resolving the referent from the conversation history.
Record the fact as an event, state, or relationship memory, including the people involved (e.g., the speaker showed the described object to another participant) when the context supports it.
Do not extract if the statement is transient, purely subjective, or the referent is ambiguous; stop after capturing the core description.

candidates.solves: Extraction often misses durable facts stated in short anaphoric replies because it expects an explicit subject in the same sentence. Apply when a reply identifies/describes an entity via a pronoun (e.g., 'It's a ...', 'That's my ...') and the referent is clear; then extract one memory candidate for the entity and involved participants. Do not apply to transient/subjective remarks, ambiguous referents, or already-captured facts.

payload.name: Extraction Pronoun Referent Resolution
payload.description: When extracting a memory candidate and the source message uses a pronoun or demonstrative (this, it, they) to refer to an entity, resolve the referent from the current conversation before storing the candidate.
content: When a user message contains a pronoun/demonstrative ('this', 'it', 'they') that carries the main predicate of a candidate memory, resolve it to the entity the speaker is discussing in that turn; if a different entity appears nearby, do not attach the predicate to that entity.

Before accepting an extraction candidate, confirm the subject and object are explicit non-pronominal entities from the session; if the referent is uncertain, check only the current turn and immediately preceding messages, then choose the entity that best matches the predicate.

candidates.solves: Memory extraction sometimes resolves pronouns/demonstratives to the wrong nearby entity, storing a candidate about a different object than the one the speaker meant. This Skill applies when a user message uses 'this', 'it', or 'they' to refer to an entity and the candidate would record an attribute or motivation about it; it directs resolving the referent from the current turn and immediate context before storage. It does not apply when the message uses explicit nouns or the referent is unambiguous.

payload.name: Resolve-pronoun-referents-in-extraction
payload.description: When extracting a memory during construction and the user message uses 'this', 'it', or 'that' without a named entity, use to resolve the referent to the current topic and avoid substituting entities from earlier unrelated context.
content: When a candidate memory is extracted from a message containing a pronoun or demonstrative ('it', 'this', 'that'), resolve it to the entity explicitly under discussion in that same exchange or immediately preceding turns.

If the candidate's subject/object names an entity not present in the same message, verify it is the true antecedent of the pronoun; if it comes from an earlier, unrelated topic, replace it with the current referent.

Before committing a memory, check that the entity in the candidate content matches the literal referent in the evidence; discard or correct candidates whose object conflicts with the unambiguous antecedent.

candidates.solves: The failure is extraction assigning a pronoun or demonstrative to an entity from an earlier, unrelated part of the conversation, so the memory's subject/object does not match the evidence. It applies when a future user message uses 'this', 'it', or 'that' to refer to the object under discussion and the extracted candidate substitutes a stale entity. It does not apply when the entity is explicitly named in the message or the referent is unambiguous within the same sentence.
